title: Events and Messaging
learning_outcomes: Explain what events and messaging contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: domain events.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Application architecture separates incoming requests, use-case rules, persistence, and external services. Patterns are useful when they clarify a dependency or invariant, not merely because they have a name. In this lesson, focus on domain events; then compare it with event dispatchers. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use events and messaging when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Application architecture separates incoming requests, use-case rules, persistence, and external services. Patterns are useful when they clarify a dependency or invariant, not merely because they have a name. For events and messaging, begin with domain events. Also distinguish event dispatchers; event listeners; asynchronous processing concepts. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
